title: Being seen versus being eligible to earn

sources.claim: Earning ad revenue on YouTube requires joining the YouTube Partner Program, which has eligibility thresholds and policies separate from simply posting videos; the thresholds have changed and should be checked in the official help page. The course does not teach the numbers.

sections.skill: Distinguish getting views from being eligible to earn on a platform

questions.prompt: Does getting views automatically mean earning ad revenue?

choices.text: No; platform programs have eligibility rules
Yes, every view always pays the creator
Yes, if the video has music

questions.correct_answer: No; platform programs have eligibility rules
questions.intro: Posting content and getting views is not the same as being ELIGIBLE TO EARN from a platform. For example, earning ad revenue on YouTube requires joining the YouTube Partner Program, which has eligibility thresholds and policies separate from simply posting videos; the thresholds have changed over time, so check the official help page rather than old articles. Platforms can also change programs. Creators often earn through several routes at once: platform programs, sponsorships, affiliate links, their own products, and services.

sections.skill: Playing music on the street versus being hired

questions.prompt: Drawing a crowd on the street is like what online?
questions.correct_answer: Getting views
questions.intro: A musician playing on a busy street may draw a crowd, but that is not the same as being booked for a paid concert. Concerts have their own requirements and contracts. Online, getting views is like drawing a crowd; joining a platform's earning program is like being booked, with its own rules to meet and keep meeting.
